title: hodd/identity/services.yaml — the hosted services registry
description: The row shape of the hosted services registry (plan 312). Every row answers seven questions in one read: how the service is raised (`unit` or `compose`), what file actually runs (`script`), what port it owns (`ports`), which kit directory it belongs to (`dir`), which runbook to open when it is down (`runbook`), whether a stop is an incident (`criticality`), and what memory it may hold (`budget`). The audit that reads this file is `bin/records/registry-audit.sh`; the law is `RULES/the-hosted-services-registry.md` and the craft page is `.agents/skills/galdr-ymirsystem/assets/registry.md`. A field this schema requires and a row does not carry is a FINDING, never a pass — the audit names the file, the row and the field.

host.description: the machine this file is written for; every row names its own host too, because one registry may describe more than one

schema.description: the registry's own header: it declares the shape its rows are written in, so the next hand writes rows that fit without reading a plan

shape.description: the schema file this header points at, repo-relative

checked_by.description: the door that judges a row against the shape

row.description: the fields a row carries, in the order a reader wants them

oneOrMany.description: a field that names one thing on a small row and several on a large one. A list is the honest form when the row really raises four units, and the audit checks every member.

id.description: the row's stable name — what `registry-audit.sh --answer <id>` takes

host.description: the machine that owns this row's files and sockets; the audit measures `script`, `dir` and the ports only on the machine the row names

unit.description: how it is raised when it is raised by systemd (user or system units). A row raised by several units names them all.

compose.description: how it is raised when it is raised by a compose file: the absolute path to that file, so `docker compose -f <file> up -d` needs no hunt

script.description: the file that actually runs — the resolved path from the unit's ExecStart or the compose service's command, never a symlink into a tree that is gone. A symlink is reported with the target it points at, because that is how the share door died unseen.

ports.description: the ports this row owns, one row per port — a port named by two rows is a fault the audit reports by naming both. An empty list is a declaration that the row owns no port (a dormant service, a job).

port.description: the singular form of `ports` for a row that owns exactly one. A row may carry `port` or `ports`, never both: two spellings of one fact is two truths.

dir.description: the kit directory the row belongs to — the runbook's first step is `cd` there, so the row must say it

runbook.description: the page to open when the service is down, home-relative or repo-relative. More than one page is separated by `·` — the audit resolves each and names the one that is missing.

criticality.description: whether a stop is an incident. `always` = a stop is an incident; `wanted` = it should be running or being finished; `dormant` = it serves nothing and only the entry says why. An unset criticality is a finding, not an answer.

budget.description: the memory this service may hold. Plan 003 (the heart estate) writes it as a measured block — `measured_mb`, `memory_ceiling_mb`, `residency` — because a budget you cannot compare with `docker stats` is a wish; a bare systemd size (`96Mi`) is accepted as the shorthand of the same fact. Both spellings are one truth: the audit reads `memory_ceiling_mb`, or the size, and never both at once.

measured.description: plan 003's measurement block: `date`, `raise` (how the service is actually raised, measured), and `containers` (memory, restarts, last error). Measurement is evidence, never the declaration: `unit` / `compose` say the door, this says what was seen.

examples.name: Excalidraw + collab + AI bridge — the whiteboard

budget.residency: always resident — a stop is an incident
